strengths: Compelling Empirical Motivation: The observation that MOTR already exhibits latent detection capabilities that are suppressed when track queries are jointly processed (AP jumping from 60.0 to 66.3 when track queries are omitted) is insightful and provides a clear motivation for the proposed approach.

Systematic Exploration of Injection Strategies: The paper provides a thorough comparative analysis of four distinct mechanisms for incorporating detection priors into transformer trackers (detector pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals), clearly demonstrating the advantages of proposal-based injection.

Detector-Free End-to-End Design: By generating 4D anchor proposals internally via a detection-only pass with shared weights, SelfMOTR preserves the end-to-end, self-contained philosophy of transformer tracking without depending on external off-the-shelf detectors like YOLOX.

Solid Performance on DanceTrack: The method achieves 69.2 HOTA and a strong 59.3 AssA / 72.5 IDF1 on DanceTrack, demonstrating that internal feature alignment is particularly beneficial for complex association tasks.
weaknesses: Subpar Results on MOT17: On the MOT17 benchmark, SelfMOTR achieves 57.5 HOTA and 70.0 MOTA, which is slightly lower than the baseline MOTR (57.8 HOTA, 73.4 MOTA) and noticeably behind other detector-free end-to-end methods such as CO-MOT (60.1 HOTA) and MeMOTR (58.8 HOTA). The explanation that MOT17 is detector-sensitive does not fully justify why SelfMOTR degrades relative to baseline MOTR.

Dual-Pass Decoder Overhead: Generating self-proposals requires executing an extra decoder pass on every frame. Even though the backbone encoder is executed only once, running the decoder twice adds computational overhead (reducing FPS from 24.8 to 20.7 on an L40S) compared to single-pass designs.

Missing Details on Default Decoder Depth: Section 4.3 and Figure 5 analyze the impact of proposal decoder depth, but the paper does not explicitly state which decoder depth configuration was adopted for the main benchmark tables (Tables 3 and 4) and Table 10 speed measurements.

strengths: Insightful empirical analysis: The observation and quantitative demonstration that MOTR possesses strong 'hidden' detection capabilities when track queries are removed (jumping from 60.0 to 66.3 mAP) provides a clear and compelling diagnosis of the detection-association conflict.

Comprehensive exploration of prior-injection strategies: The paper systematically benchmarks four distinct mechanisms for injecting detection priors (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals) in Table 2, offering valuable insights for the transformer tracking literature.

Clean, self-contained architecture: Unlike MOTRv2 and MOTRv3 which rely on separate external detectors (e.g., YOLOX), SelfMOTR generates its own priors via an internal detection-only pass with shared weights, preserving the detector-free, end-to-end design philosophy.
Strong performance on DanceTrack: The method achieves competitive results on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA, 72.5 IDF1) and reaches the highest association score (59.3 AssA) among end-to-end trackers.

Thorough ablations and efficiency analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablations covering proposal sources, threshold sensitivity, data scaling, decoder depth, and inference frame rate (showing that sharing the heavy encoder limits runtime degradation to only ~17%).
weaknesses: Underwhelming performance on MOT17: While the method shows clear benefits on DanceTrack, the performance on MOT17 (57.5 HOTA) is slightly below the original MOTR baseline (57.8 HOTA) and trails other end-to-end models like CO-MOT (60.1 HOTA) and MOTRv3 (60.2 HOTA).

Dual-pass decoder overhead during training and inference: Although the heavy visual backbone is executed only once, running two decoder passes per frame inevitably increases computational and memory overhead during training and reduces inference throughput.

Missing training cost details: The paper reports inference speed on a Tesla L40S, but omits discussion of the training wall-clock time and peak GPU memory footprint compared to the standard single-pass MOTR training pipeline.

Scope limited to vanilla MOTR: The authors acknowledge that SelfMOTR is only instantiated on top of the original MOTR baseline, leaving open whether the self-proposal concept translates into additional gains when integrated into stronger recent baselines (e.g., MeMOTR, CO-MOT).

strengths: Clear motivation and empirical grounding: The paper clearly identifies and dissects the detection–association conflict in MOTR-like architectures, convincingly demonstrating through Figure 2 and Table 1 that latent detection capability is suppressed when track queries are activated.

Systematic exploration of prior-injection strategies: Section 3.1 and Table 2 offer a clean, methodical analysis comparing four different mechanisms to inject detection priors (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals), providing valuable diagnostic insights for the tracking community.

Detector-free design: Unlike MOTRv2/v3, which rely heavily on external detectors like YOLOX, SelfMOTR preserves the self-contained, end-to-end nature of the tracker by recycling the model's own internal detection proposals.
Competitive performance on DanceTrack: The proposed framework demonstrates clear gains on DanceTrack, achieving 69.2 HOTA and leading association accuracy (59.3 AssA) among end-to-end trackers.
weaknesses: Performance degradation on MOT17: While the central hypothesis is that self-proposals alleviate the detection bottleneck, on MOT17 (Table 4) SelfMOTR attains only 57.5 HOTA and 57.3 DetA, underperforming even the vanilla MOTR baseline (57.8 HOTA, 60.3 DetA) and lagging significantly behind concurrent detector-free methods like CO-MOT (60.1 HOTA). This raises serious doubts about the generalizability of the approach across diverse tracking domains.

Limited architectural novelty: Decoupling proposal generation from tracking and passing 4D bounding box anchors into decoder queries heavily mirrors the mechanism established by MOTRv2, simply replacing the external detector with an extra forward pass of the model's own decoder.

Incomplete computational and training profiling: Although inference FPS is reported in Table 10, the paper does not report GFLOPs, peak GPU memory footprint, or the overhead on training convergence time incurred by computing two decoder forward passes and additional Hungarian matchings per frame.

Narrow benchmark coverage given conflicting results: Because results improve on DanceTrack but regress on MOT17, the evaluation on only two datasets is insufficient to draw firm conclusions. Validating on additional benchmarks (e.g., BDD100K or SportsMOT) is needed to properly substantiate the claimed benefits.

strengths: Compelling motivation and systematic exploratory analysis: The paper identifies and clearly demonstrates the latent detection capacity in MOTR when track queries are omitted (Figure 2), and thoroughly benchmarks four distinct mechanisms for injecting detection priors (Table 1) before arriving at the proposed self-generating design.

Detector-free end-to-end design: Unlike MOTRv2/v3, which rely on external object detectors (such as YOLOX) and thereby compromise the self-contained nature of end-to-end MOT, SelfMOTR generates natively aligned spatial anchors internally through a lightweight detection-only pass using the shared decoder.

Insightful diagnostic analysis: The paper introduces Track Attention Mass and normalized Shannon entropy to evaluate query dynamics across decoder layers. This provides valuable empirical insight into query interference and attention polarization in transformer decoders during joint detection and association.

Strong performance on challenging dynamic datasets: SelfMOTR achieves state-of-the-art results on Bird Flock Tracking (71.1 HOTA) and AnimalTrack (45.5 HOTA), while remaining highly competitive on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA, leading association score AssA of 59.3 among end-to-end trackers).
weaknesses: Computational overhead of dual decoder passes: Although the feature encoder is only executed once per frame, running the decoder twice increases computation and drops inference speed from 24.8 FPS to 20.7 FPS on an L40S GPU.

Performance on dense pedestrian tracking (MOT17): As shown in Table 5, SelfMOTR (57.5 / 58.4 HOTA) lags slightly behind other recent end-to-end methods such as CO-MOT (60.1) and MOTRv3 (60.2), and still exhibits a substantial gap compared to non-end-to-end trackers.

Conceptual similarity to cascade/two-stage decoders: Decoupling proposal extraction and refinement into a two-pass decoding scheme shares conceptual overlap with two-stage DETR architectures and TransTrack, which somewhat reduces the algorithmic novelty of the underlying pipeline despite the specific focus on query interference.

strengths: Clear motivation and insightful diagnosis: The paper provides a clear empirical demonstration that joint detection-association transformers retain strong latent detection capacity when track queries are omitted, and it proposes an intuitive, detector-free mechanism to harness this capacity.

Analytical contribution via Track Attention Mass: The introduction of Track Attention Mass and normalized Shannon entropy offers a valuable diagnostic lens for inspecting self-attention dynamics between detect and track queries, revealing the mechanism behind query interference in end-to-end MOT.

Detector-free unified design: By having the model generate its own spatial proposals internally via a lightweight detection pass, SelfMOTR avoids relying on external, off-the-shelf detectors (such as YOLOX in MOTRv2/v3) while maintaining competitive tracking performance.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across diverse benchmarks (DanceTrack, Bird Flock Tracking, AnimalTrack, MOT17) with thorough ablation studies analyzing prior injection strategies, proposal thresholds, decoder depths, and runtime efficiency.
weaknesses: Dual-pass computational overhead: Generating self-proposals requires an additional decoder pass per frame. Although the backbone encoder is shared and FPS remains reasonable (20.7 FPS vs. 24.8 FPS baseline), this still introduces sequential decoder computation that impacts overall efficiency.

Incremental performance gains on standard benchmarks: On DanceTrack test, SelfMOTR achieves 69.2 HOTA, which is on par with CO-MOT (69.4) and slightly below MOTRv2 (69.9). Furthermore, on MOT17 (Appendix Table 5), SelfMOTR achieves 58.4 HOTA, lagging behind existing end-to-end baselines like CO-MOT (60.1) and MOTRv3 (60.2).

Residual heuristics in proposal selection: While aiming for a clean end-to-end design, the proposal filtering stage still relies on hand-tuned hyper-parameters, notably the proposal confidence threshold c_prop and the heuristic appending of a fixed number of learned proposal anchors (N_learned = 10) to compensate for false negatives.

strengths: Insightful diagnostic analysis of query interference: The paper provides a clear and intuitive study of the detection-association conflict in MOTR. In particular, the introduction of Track Attention Mass and normalized Shannon entropy offers meaningful insight into how self-attention becomes polarized between track context and discovery queries in standard joint decoding.

Self-contained detector-free formulation: Unlike prior works (such as MOTRv2 and MOTRv3) that depend on external off-the-shelf detectors like YOLOX, SelfMOTR generates spatial proposals natively from its own internal representations, preserving an end-to-end design while avoiding complex external pipelines.

Strong empirical performance on challenging non-linear datasets: The method achieves very strong results on benchmarks characterized by dynamic motions and heavy target deformations, attaining state-of-the-art results among end-to-end trackers on the Bird Flock Tracking (BFT) dataset (71.1 HOTA) and AnimalTrack (45.5 HOTA), while remaining competitive on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA).

Comprehensive ablation and progression study: The experimental progression in Table 1 (comparing detector pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, and anchor proposals) systematically justifies why generating explicit internal 4D anchor proposals is the most effective prior mechanism.
weaknesses: Two-pass decoding increases computational latency: Generating proposals via an initial detection pass requires running the transformer decoder twice per frame. Although the backbone features are shared and the decoder pass can be truncated, inference speed drops (e.g., from 24.8 FPS to 20.7 FPS on an L40S GPU), moving the architecture closer to a two-stage cascade rather than a purely unified single-stage tracker.

Performance on standard pedestrian benchmarks (e.g., MOT17) remains limited: On MOT17 (Table 5), SelfMOTR achieves 58.4 HOTA, lagging behind competing end-to-end trackers such as CO-MOT (60.1 HOTA) and MOTRv3 (60.2 HOTA), and continuing to trail tracking-by-detection and graph-based baselines by a noticeable margin.

Introduction of hand-tuned proposal filtering heuristics: Filtering self-proposals with a fixed confidence threshold (c_prop = 0.05) and appending a fixed set of learned anchors (N_learned = 10) reintroduces heuristic hyperparameter tuning that pure end-to-end query-based trackers strive to eliminate.

Conceptual connection to LLM attention sinks is largely metaphorical: While the attention mass and entropy diagnostic is empirically informative, framing this phenomenon around large language model 'attention sinks' is largely descriptive and lacks formal theoretical connection to the autoregressive sink dynamics found in LLMs.
